name: Amazon Redshift
description: AWS's data warehouse, evolved from provisioned MPP clusters to serverless with separated storage (RA3) and deep AWS integration (Spectrum over S3, zero-ETL from Aurora). Pick it when the estate is firmly AWS; head-to-head, Snowflake and BigQuery usually beat it on ergonomics.

name: Amazon S3
description: The object store that defined the API the whole industry now speaks; eleven-nines durability, endless tiering options, and first-target support from every data tool. On AWS it isn't a choice, it's the substrate — S3 Tables even bakes Iceberg in natively.

name: Apache Arrow
description: The in-memory columnar standard that lets engines and libraries (DuckDB, Polars, pandas, Spark) share data with zero copying, plus wire protocols like Arrow Flight. You rarely 'choose' Arrow directly — you benefit from it whenever your stack is built on it.

name: Apache Avro
description: A row-oriented serialization format with schemas stored alongside data and well-defined schema evolution rules. The de facto payload format for Kafka (with a schema registry) and a solid choice for write-heavy pipelines and data interchange, complementing columnar formats at rest.

name: Apache Doris
description: An MPP real-time OLAP database with MySQL-protocol compatibility, big in the Chinese internet sector and increasingly visible elsewhere. Similar trade-offs to StarRocks (its fork): good joins and easy onboarding for MySQL-fluent teams.

name: Apache Druid
description: A real-time OLAP store built for streaming ingestion (Kafka/Kinesis) with sub-second slice-and-dice over event data, proven at large scale (Netflix, Confluent). Powerful but operationally heavy — its many node roles mean you should want its exact strengths before signing up.

name: Apache Hudi
description: The table format that pioneered incremental upsert/delete pipelines on the data lake (Uber lineage), with merge-on-read tables and built-in ingestion tooling. Still the strongest at record-level streaming upserts, but it has lost the ecosystem race to Iceberg for general use.

name: Apache Iceberg
description: The open table format that has become the industry's neutral standard for lakehouse tables: ACID snapshots, hidden partitioning, schema evolution, and a REST catalog spec every engine is adopting. Pick it by default for new lakehouse builds — vendor momentum (Snowflake, Databricks, AWS) has consolidated behind it.

name: Apache ORC
description: The Hive-lineage columnar format with strong compression and built-in indexes, historically favored in Hortonworks/Hive shops. Technically excellent but ecosystem-wise it lost to Parquet — choose it only when an existing Hive/Trino estate already standardized on it.

name: Apache Paimon
description: A newer lake table format designed around an LSM-tree architecture for high-throughput streaming upserts, developed hand-in-glove with Apache Flink. Pick it for Flink-centric streaming lakehouses; elsewhere Iceberg remains the safer bet.

name: Apache Parquet
description: The universal columnar file format for analytics: efficient compression, predicate pushdown via column statistics, and support in essentially every engine and library. The unquestioned default for analytical data at rest — every table format sits on top of it.

name: Apache Pinot
description: LinkedIn's real-time OLAP engine, designed for user-facing analytics at extreme query concurrency (its star-tree index is the signature feature). Pick it over Druid when thousands of concurrent low-latency queries from an application are the workload; StarTree offers the managed version.

name: Apache Polaris
description: The Iceberg REST catalog Snowflake open-sourced and donated to the ASF, offering vendor-neutral, credential-vending access control across engines. A leading candidate for the 'open catalog' role in Iceberg-first architectures — young, but with serious backing.

name: Apache Thrift
description: Facebook-lineage serialization plus RPC framework, still embedded in older infrastructure (notably the Hive Metastore protocol). For new work Protobuf/gRPC has won this space — you deal with Thrift because something you depend on already speaks it.

name: AWS Glue Data Catalog
description: AWS's serverless, Hive-compatible metastore shared by Athena, EMR, Redshift Spectrum, and Lake Formation, with growing Iceberg REST support. The path of least resistance for table metadata on AWS — you use it because you're on AWS, not because you chose it.

name: Azure Blob Storage
description: Azure's massively scalable object storage for unstructured data, with hot/cool/archive tiers and the foundation for the data lake. When the hierarchical namespace is enabled it becomes Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) Gen2, the standard analytics-optimized layer. It's the direct analog to Amazon S3 and Google Cloud Storage; pick it as the default landing zone and lakehouse storage on Azure.

name: Azure Data Explorer
description: A fully managed, high-performance analytics engine for log, telemetry, and time-series data, queried with the Kusto Query Language (KQL). It's Azure's answer to Amazon Timestream / analytical stores like ClickHouse or Druid, and the engine underneath Log Analytics and Microsoft Fabric's Real-Time Intelligence. Pick it when you need fast interactive exploration over huge streams of append-only observability or IoT data.

name: Azure Data Lake Storage
description: Azure Blob Storage with a hierarchical namespace (Gen2), giving filesystem semantics — atomic renames, POSIX-ish ACLs — that analytics engines want. The standard lake layer on Azure and the storage under Fabric's OneLake.

name: Azure Synapse Analytics
description: Azure's integrated analytics platform bundling a dedicated SQL warehouse (ex SQL DW), serverless SQL, and Spark pools. Still widely deployed, but Microsoft's investment has clearly shifted to Fabric — think twice before starting anything new on Synapse.

name: Backblaze B2
description: Low-cost cloud object storage exposing both a native B2 API and an S3-compatible API, positioned as one of the cheapest alternatives to Amazon S3 for backup and cold data. Its differentiator is aggressively low per-GB storage pricing plus free egress to partners like Cloudflare via the Bandwidth Alliance, making it a common cold-storage and archive tier.

name: BigQuery
description: Google's serverless data warehouse: no clusters to size, petabyte scans on demand, and tight integration with GCP's ML and streaming stack. The obvious pick on Google Cloud; on-demand pricing per byte scanned makes partitioning and cost hygiene mandatory.

name: Ceph
description: A unified software-defined storage system providing object (S3-compatible RGW), block, and file interfaces from one self-healing cluster. Pick it when you're building serious on-prem storage infrastructure and have (or will hire) the operational depth it demands.

name: ClickHouse
description: The fastest widely-used columnar OLAP database: brutal single-query speed, great compression, and a huge function library, born at Yandex and now with a strong managed cloud. The default pick for real-time and log/event analytics when you can model around its eventual-consistency merges and limited join ergonomics.

name: Cloudflare R2
description: S3-compatible object storage that runs on Cloudflare's global edge network, the small-cloud analog to Amazon S3, Azure Blob, and Google Cloud Storage. Its defining differentiator is zero egress fees: you pay for storage and operations but never for data transfer out, which makes it attractive for serving assets and data lakes with heavy read traffic.

name: CSV
description: The lowest common denominator of data exchange: human-readable, universally supported, and standardized only loosely (RFC 4180). Unbeatable for interoperability with non-technical partners; a liability for anything else — no types, no schema, and quoting edge cases everywhere.

name: Databricks SQL
description: Databricks' warehouse experience over the lakehouse: Photon-accelerated SQL on Delta/Iceberg tables with serverless warehouses and standard BI connectivity. Pick it when Databricks is already your platform — you get warehouse-grade SQL without copying data out of the lake.

name: Delta Lake
description: Databricks' open table format bringing ACID transactions, time travel, and upserts to Parquet on object storage, with the deepest Spark integration of the formats. The natural choice inside the Databricks ecosystem; interoperability layers (UniForm) now blur the line with Iceberg.

name: DigitalOcean Spaces
description: S3-compatible object storage from DigitalOcean aimed at developers and small teams, the small-cloud analog to Amazon S3. Its differentiator is a built-in CDN and simple flat-rate pricing that bundles a generous storage and transfer allowance, making it a low-friction choice for serving static assets and backups alongside DigitalOcean Droplets.

name: Exasol
description: An in-memory columnar MPP database with a long record of topping TPC-H benchmarks, popular in European enterprises. Pick it when raw query speed on-prem (or self-managed in cloud) is the requirement and a niche vendor relationship is acceptable.

name: Firebolt
description: A cloud warehouse engineered for low-latency, high-concurrency analytics via aggressive indexing and Postgres-dialect SQL. Pick it for customer-facing analytics where sub-second dashboards on large data must be served cheaply — a niche between classic warehouses and real-time OLAP engines.

name: Google Cloud Storage
description: GCP's object storage: S3-comparable durability and tiering with a single global namespace and strong BigQuery/Dataproc integration. The default lake substrate on Google Cloud; its interoperability mode also speaks the S3 API.

name: Greenplum
description: A Postgres-based open-source MPP warehouse that had a strong on-prem run under Pivotal/VMware. Broadcom closed the open-source repository in 2024, leaving the community to forks (Cloudberry) — avoid for new builds, plan exits for existing ones.

name: HDFS
description: The Hadoop Distributed File System — the storage layer the big-data era was built on, with data locality for co-located compute. Still serving existing on-prem Hadoop estates, but object storage has decisively won: don't build anything new on it.

name: Hetzner Object Storage
description: S3-compatible object storage from Hetzner, a German provider, positioned as a low-cost alternative to Amazon S3. Its differentiator is EU-based data residency and Hetzner's characteristically low, predictable pricing including cheap egress, making it appealing for cost-sensitive European workloads with data-sovereignty requirements.

name: Hive Metastore
description: The Hadoop-era metadata service that became the accidental standard: for a decade nearly every engine (Spark, Trino, Presto) spoke its Thrift API to find tables. Still everywhere in existing platforms, but new builds should prefer a REST-based Iceberg catalog.

name: IBM Netezza
description: The pioneering data-warehouse appliance (FPGA-accelerated), now living on as IBM Netezza Performance Server on Cloud Pak. Encountered almost exclusively as a legacy estate to migrate off — nobody starts here in 2026.

name: JSON / NDJSON
description: The universal semi-structured interchange format; the newline-delimited variant (NDJSON/JSON Lines) makes it streamable and splittable for data pipelines. The default for APIs, logs, and event payloads — convert to a columnar format before analytics at any real scale.

name: Lakekeeper
description: A lightweight, Rust-built Apache-licensed Iceberg REST catalog with Postgres as its backing store and OpenFGA-based authorization. Attractive as a self-hosted, no-JVM catalog for teams who want Iceberg without adopting a vendor platform — still early-days.

name: Microsoft Fabric
description: Microsoft's all-in-one SaaS analytics platform unifying warehouse, lakehouse (OneLake on Delta), data engineering, and Power BI under a single capacity-based license. The strategic path for Microsoft shops; the breadth is real but the pieces vary in maturity, so validate your specific workloads.

name: MinIO
description: The leading self-hosted, S3-compatible object store: a single Go binary that scales to high-performance distributed clusters. The default answer for on-prem and air-gapped data lakes; note the 2025 gutting of the community console pushed some users toward forks and alternatives.

name: MotherDuck
description: A serverless warehouse built on DuckDB with a hybrid execution model that splits queries between your laptop and the cloud. Compelling for small-to-mid data teams who love DuckDB locally and want shared, managed storage without Snowflake-class cost or ceremony.

name: Oracle Cloud Object Storage
description: Object storage on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure with S3-compatible and native APIs, the OCI analog to Amazon S3 and Azure Blob. Its differentiator is enterprise-grade tiering (Standard, Infrequent Access, and Archive) tightly integrated with OCI's data and analytics services and Oracle's aggressive egress pricing relative to the big three.

name: Project Nessie
description: A transactional catalog for Iceberg that adds Git-like semantics — branches, tags, and multi-table commits — enabling isolated dev/test on production data (Dremio-sponsored). Pick it when data-as-code workflows matter more than broad vendor support.

name: Protocol Buffers
description: Google's compact binary serialization with schema-first codegen across languages, and the wire format underneath gRPC. The default for service-to-service payloads and increasingly common on Kafka; less convenient than Avro for dynamic, registry-driven data pipelines.

name: Rockset
description: A real-time analytics service built on converged indexing over RocksDB, notable for SQL on semi-structured data with no schema management. OpenAI acquired the company in 2024 and the public service was shut down — listed for historical/migration context only.

name: Snowflake
description: The cloud data warehouse that defined the category: separated storage/compute, near-zero administration, instant scaling, and easy data sharing across accounts and clouds. The safe enterprise default when analyst productivity outweighs cost control — its consumption pricing rewards governance discipline.

name: StarRocks
description: A Doris-descended MPP OLAP engine (now Linux Foundation) whose distinguishing strength is fast multi-table joins — no forced denormalization — plus direct lakehouse querying over Iceberg/Hudi. A strong ClickHouse rival when your schema is genuinely relational.

name: Teradata
description: The original enterprise MPP warehouse, still running mission-critical analytics in banks, telcos, and retailers, with a cloud offering in VantageCloud. Formidable workload management, but green-field selections are rare — it's primarily a migration source these days.

name: Unity Catalog
description: Databricks' governance-grade catalog — tables, files, models, and lineage with fine-grained access control — open-sourced under Apache 2.0 in 2024. Essentially mandatory on Databricks; the OSS server is young, so treat the managed and open flavors as different maturity levels.

name: Vertica
description: A columnar MPP warehouse (Stonebraker's C-Store lineage, now OpenText) known for strong compression and projections-based query speed. Still solid for on-prem columnar analytics, but momentum has moved to cloud warehouses and ClickHouse-style engines.

name: XML
description: The elder statesman of structured interchange, with mature schema (XSD) and transformation (XSLT) tooling. Verbose and unloved in modern data stacks, but unavoidable in B2B, finance, healthcare, and government feeds — plan parsers accordingly.
